newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian police launch raids to curb gang wars.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian police launch raids to curb gang wars.

text.p: As a gangland-style murder on Friday followed four bombings in six days, police said they have detained over 100 people in raids on bars and nightclubs in the Hungarian capital.
Tourism officials are beginning to worry about the latest spate of bombings.
"This gang war has got to the point a civilised European city cannot tolerate," General Janos Bodracska, head of Budapest police, told a news conference.
Police said a Budapest gang leader was shot at point-blank range on Friday apparently victim of a war between groups in organised crime .
The man, Jozsef Prisztas, was shot with a 9mm handgun while sitting in his jeep, police sources told Reuters.
Since Saturday, four hand grenades have exploded in Budapest, causing damage but no injuries.
Bodracska added that during the last two nights police raided every nightclub in the city, detaining 25 people on Wednesday night and 100 on Thursday night.
"I hope we will shortly be able to name the suspects of the bombings," Bodracska said.
National and Budapest police have set up a 137-strong task force to deal with the gang war, National Police Chief Sandor Pinter said.
Press reports have speculated that the grenades could be part of two crates that disappeared from a military unit at the end of 1995.
An officer working on the case said he could not confirm this but the origin of the grenades was a strong lead in the cases.

"This is one of the main lines we are following, but saying any more about it would amount to alerting the suspects," Lieutenant-Colonel Elek Katai of the National Police's Homicide Squad told Reuters.
Police have registered 26 explosions this year in Hungary, of which 16 were in Budapest, Katai said.
Many of the grenades were of a type extensively used in former Warsaw Pact countries and during the Yugoslav wars, police said.
Katai added that grenades were a new weapon for criminals but autumn is the customary season for gangs to compete for influence in Budapest's underworld.
"It is the end of the summer, gangs are returning from Balaton (Hungary's most popular summer resort), and the city is becoming too small for all of them," Katai said.

Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze said on Friday he had briefed the government about the investigation at a cabinet meeting and added that Prime Minister Gyula Horn was constantly monitoring developments.
"Speaking for myself, I would not like to go to a city where four bombings happened within a week," Tibor Sivo, general secretary of the Association of Tourism Companies, told Reuters.
He added, however, that he had not received more enquiries than usual about Hungary's public safety from foreign tour operators or embassies.
